items.description: Mortgage Rates Move Slightly Lower By: Matthew Graham 50 Min, 18 Secs ago Mortgage rates fell for the second straight day with help from lower prices in oil/diesel and the stock market. These shouldn't be viewed as reliable sources of inspiration as rates often move in the opposite direction. There was simply little else to justify today's improvement and the correlations happened to line up fairly well. While rates are indeed lower, the pace of the improvement has been slow so far this week. At 7.46%, the average top-tier 30yr fixed rate is still nearly 0.20% higher compared to the beginning of last week. There were no big-ticket events on the economic calendar and the release of the minutes from the Fed's most recent meeting (3 weeks ago) had no impact. In general, the 2nd half of November can be fairly random for rates due to idiosyncrasies associated with the holiday trading environment. items.title: BTR Operators Push For Treasury To Loosen Rules As Consolidation Looms
items.description: The build-to-rent sector is facing a second round of wrangling with the government after a hard-fought battle with lawmakers over the summer to keep the industry from facing steep regulations as part of the housing bill that made its way through Congress . BTR operators and industry advocates are pushing for changes to proposed rules from the Department of the Treasury that will dictate how the restrictions on BTR operators from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act are implemented. Operators in the sector say the rules could hamper new development and, regardless of what’s adjusted, expect consolidation to sweep across the sector. “Hopefully that gets adjusted, because that will have a severe impact on capital flows and ultimately the building of new homes and new rental communities,” Richard Ross , CEO of Atlanta-based Quinn Residences , said of the proposed rules. Unsplash/Michael Tuszynski The proposed regulations require large institutional investors, which are defined in the original legislation as firms with at least 350 single-family rental units, to adopt written BTR programs before they purchase a community and would preclude BTR operators from purchasing properties more than 18 months after the home received its certificate of occupancy. Ross, whose firm has developed or purchased 5,200 homes across 34 communities since its founding in 2020, wrote in a letter submitted as a public comment to Treasury that it can frequently take two years or more to stabilize a newly built community. The two new rules would make it more difficult for homebuilders to sell excess inventory to build-to-rent operators, hampering activity in a pool of properties that BTR operators have long dipped into, Ross told Bisnow . His letter was one of more than 100 public comments filed so far. Other operators and industry groups, including the nonpartisan trade association National Rental Home Council , are still crafting their own submissions, CEO Adrianne Todman said. The public comment period closes on Nov. 23. “The Treasury Department has put forward some thoughtful rules where they're trying to thread the needle very carefully by making sure they are properly implementing the legislative ban on investors being able to buy homes but also making sure that it's not having any detrimental impacts to the housing marketplace and particularly the rental marketplace,” Todman said. The push to shift the rules follows the first bout of uncertainty that shrouded the BTR sector when the Road to Housing legislation was originally being debated. The bill debuted with strict restrictions on the BTR business model that threatened to upend the sector. It took intense lobbying for the rules to shift. Investment in the sector was severely scaled back during that debate, as investors waited to see what the final legislation would include. “When there was a threat to being able to build new rental supply via build-to-rent, we saw that there was millions of dollars and thousands of units that went on the sidelines and that those resources were frozen,” Todman said. “Those resources are thawing out a bit, and we want to make sure that they thaw out even more.” The push for clear guidelines gained new momentum after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Some senators-elect ran on campaigns explicitly against corporate ownership of homes, including James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa. Talarico’s website includes a call to “ban Wall Street from buying up housing stock to enrich wealthy investors while making it harder for families to afford homes,” and Turek’s platform includes a call to ban private equity firms from purchasing single-family homes. The Road to Housing legislation adds new compliance standards and an element of federal oversight, including public reporting requirements for large operators, that are expected to lead to a wave of buyouts and mergers across the sector. The consolidation is likely coming regardless of where Treasury lands on its rules, as smaller players are squeezed by costs that large operators that benefit from economies of scale can more easily absorb. “You put it all together, it's just a tougher backdrop for them to really justify their existence,” said Haendel St. Juste , equity research analyst at Mizuho , who upgraded the two major publicly traded single-family rental firms to outperform in September. Unsplash/Nate Johnston New compliance costs for operators with at least 350 units but not thousands will raise operating costs for smaller BTR firms around the same time that the private equity funds backing those platforms reach the end of their lives. A substantial amount of the debt backing private BTR and SFR firms was issued around five to seven years ago and is reaching the end of its natural life cycle, leaving operators facing significantly higher debt service costs to stay in business, St. Juste said. Nontraded SFR REIT VineBrook Homes Trust suspended share buybacks earlier this month after ending a tender offer that drew three times as many shares as the REIT sought to buy. VineBrook, which has 20,500 units in 21 states, flagged an upcoming $650.8M debt maturity within a year as a driving factor behind the shift in strategy. For Invitation Homes and American Homes 4 Rent , the two biggest publicly traded single-family rental firms, the legislation creates a unique and sizable rollup opportunity, St. Juste wrote in a September analysis. The two REITs have trailed the broader REIT index by about 13 percentage points this year, according to Mizuho’s September report, and investors see upside potential in the wide gap that exists between the firms’ public valuations and the value of the properties in their portfolios. The REITs have been using that gap to sell homes and buy back stock at an attractive valuation, a trend that is expected to continue into 2027. Economic Overview Life sciences employment across the Bay Area, according to Lightcast, ended the third quarter of 2026 at 104,400 positions, with some of the largest employers in the region being BioMarin Pharmaceutical, Amgen, and Gilead Sciences. The Bay Area continues to be the top U.S. market in employment with Boston (101,900) and New York (87,000) following. Life sciences in the local region partially thrives from funding to universities from the National Institutes of Health (NIH); in the third quarter, Stanford ranked eighth while UCSF took the second spot, based on dollars awarded nationally. Venture capital funding into Bay Area life sciences companies in the third quarter came in at $2.1 billion, according to Pitchbook. During that period, Bay-Area headquartered companies received 28.0% of the total U.S. funding. The largest deals in the region went to San Francisco-based Chai Discovery at $400.0 million and South San Francisco-based Encoded at $275.0 million. Supply & Demand: Rising Vacancy in the East Bay The overall vacancy rate at the end of the third quarter of 2026 was 28.5%, down 20 basis points (bps) from 28.7% in the previous quarter and down 60 bps from 29.1% one year ago. Direct vacancy stayed relatively flat around 11.5 million square feet (msf). Sublease vacancy was consistent quarter-over-quarter as well at 2.5 msf. East Bay Oakland vacancy increased the most year-over-year, up 230 bps or 255,104 square feet (sf) from the same quarter last year, largely due to the delivery of new construction projects that completed in 2025. Additional consolidations also contributed to vacancy over the last 18 months. There was 828,511 sf of total leasing activity (new leases and renewals) for the third quarter, an increase from the 748,556 sf in the second quarter, and up from 783,364 sf during the same period last year. New leases made up 75.4% or 624,859 sf of the activity, while renewals made up the rest at 24.6% or 203,652 sf. New leases with Lilly Gateway Labs (South San Francisco) and Structure Therapeutics (South San Francisco) contributed significantly to activity this quarter. Supply: Eight Large-Scale Projects Completed in 2025 & 2026 There were eight ground-up developments, all speculative and totaling approximately 2.0 msf, completed since the beginning of 2025. These included Avia Labs (315,000 sf) in Millbrae, SPUR Phase I (330,350 sf) in South San Francisco, and The Landing (503,500 sf) in Burlingame. Along with those were 1030 Brittan Ave (108,134 sf) in San Carlos which was preleased to MBC Biolabs in 2022, Portal 405 (240,000 sf) in San Carlos, Menlo Park Labs (268,468 sf), and 200 Twin Dolphin (234,000 sf) in Redwood Shores. Finally, the last project that completed construction was ELCO Yards – The Shop in Redwood City, totaling 225,878 sf. Conversions were more active in the Bay Area in the third quarter with roughly 336,433 sf in the pipeline. Projects under renovation are 2400-2470 Charleston Road (108,474 sf) in Mountain View, Island Parkway (179,172 sf) in Redwood Shores, and 901 California Avenue (54,800 sf) in Palo Alto. Pricing: Rents Remain Muted The overall average asking rate for Bay Area life sciences space closed out the third quarter at $5.53 per square foot (psf) on a monthly triple net basis, a decrease from $5.93 psf one year ago. Overall average asking rates have been steadily decreasing in in the Santa Clara County and San Mateo County markets with the former having the largest change from $4.58 psf in the second quarter of 2026 to $4.32 psf in the third quarter. San Francisco County recorded a quarterly increase to its average asking rates due to several higher-end spaces that came to market including 1700 Owens Street. Tenants in the Market: There were 54 life sciences tenants in the market throughout the Bay Area at the close of the third quarter of 2026, totaling 2.4 msf with an average requirement size of 44,676 sf. San Mateo County counted the most tenant requirements at 35, while also averaging the highest requirement size at 50,929 sf. items.title: Nvidia Tops Forecasts In First Report Without Jensen Huang, But Gets Choosier About Backing Data Centers
items.description: On paper, Nvidia’s first earnings report without Jensen Huang looked a lot like the ones with him. Almost nothing else about it did. The world’s most valuable chipmaker has spent recent weeks fighting on nearly every front — its founder’s abrupt exit, a national security probe, midterm backlash against data centers, and a Wall Street sell-off fueled by fears of an AI bubble. Its market value has fallen by roughly $2T since October to about $3.75T. Nvidia Nvidia Voyager headquarters in Santa Clara, California On Tuesday’s earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress argued that none of it has slowed the business. Asked whether Democrats’ takeover of Congress could cool artificial intelligence spending, she said customers had spent the past week asking how to get more chips and that demand will hold “not only in the ’27 perspective, but moving to the ’28 as well.” As for the turmoil at the top, “from a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. On the numbers, it was. Nvidia brought in $115.8B in revenue in the three months ending on Oct. 25, double a year earlier and nearly $7B more than Wall Street expected. Data center chips accounted for $107.6B of it. Nvidia expects about $130B this quarter, and Kress raised her forecast for next fiscal year to roughly 75% growth from 70%. Shares, which closed down 0.4% at $155.46, were up roughly 4% in after-hours trading as of 7 p.m. ET on Tuesday. In 49 minutes, one of the most anticipated earnings calls in recent memory touched on almost everything that matters to data center owners, developers, lenders and even Washington: whether demand is holding up, which projects Nvidia will help finance, who gets its scarce chips, who will run the company and whether it will keep selling to China. On China, the answer for now is no. Nvidia has stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips there, a business worth $2.4B last quarter, and its outlook assumes no China data center sales. For commercial real estate, few earnings reports matter more. Nvidia’s chips are the costliest item inside a data center, and the promise of ever more of them has sent developers racing to buy land and lock up power from the New Mexico desert to southern Ohio, a construction boom backed by an estimated $1.3T of debt . Tuesday’s report was the industry’s first look at whether the engine of the boom keeps running without the man who built it. By Kress’ account, it does. Nvidia compute “remains fully utilized across every hyperscaler and neocloud we serve,” she said. Hopper chips, now two generations old, are being rerented at up to twice their original price, and the cloud industry’s backlog has grown to $2.5T from $2T three months ago. The bigger shift was about money. Nvidia hasn’t just sold chips into the boom — it has helped pay for it , with $118B in guarantees outstanding, including $105B for OpenAI’s planned campus at SB Energy’s Ports-Pike site in Ohio. Kress said it will be “disciplined in how we commit capital” and “disciplined and selective” in backing neoclouds, the younger cloud providers that rent out its chips. “As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” she said. For developers, the fine print matters. Pressed by Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon, Kress said Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only once a project is financed, built and ready for chips. If a developer falls behind, “our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore.” Nvidia, in other words, isn’t taking on construction risk. When it does help, Kress said, a top priority will be the real estate itself — the land, the power hookup and the building shell that must exist before a single chip arrives. She called that “a great asset for anyone to hold.” Before Kress said a word, board Chair Harvey Jones closed the door that Huang had cracked open that morning, when the founder said he would be “honored” to return. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said, and would take no questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” No analyst tried. The board has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent CEO, but, Jones said, “we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” Huang resigned Thursday amid reports of a relationship with a former executive of Singapore data center firm Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China, and of alleged affairs with Nvidia employees. The board has since formed a national security and export control oversight committee. Huang is due to give closed-door testimony Dec. 1 to three House committees investigating what they called “a potential breach of our national security.” The Securities and Exchange Commission is also investigating whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday , citing people familiar with the matter. The scandal has already reached data centers. The U.S. Commerce Department first found Nvidia chips inside a Megaspeed facility in Malaysia, and on Monday, it issued a rule requiring data centers to get a license before renting advanced AI chip capacity to Chinese companies. Kress said Nvidia is still studying the rule, but “with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong.” Lenders are flinching, too. HSBC sold a $300M slice of Project Jupiter’s construction loan at prices in the mid-80s, Bloomberg reported, after Oracle sent the developer a force majeure notice . By the end, Kress sounded less like a finance chief than a coach rallying her team. “Our customers and our partners are with us,” she told analysts. “We’ve got this.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Colette Kress , Jensen Huang , Nvidia

items.description: Healthcare providers are searching near and far for suitable space in Greater Boston's ultratight medical office market, leading them into new areas and types of properties. Boston's 28M SF medical office market last quarter had an occupancy rate of 94.4%, according to Avison Young — the highest rate of the 20 largest markets and above the national average of 92.2%. Though demand for outpatient medical space is extremely high, new development hasn't kept up. Avison Young found that Boston had 19K SF of new medical office space delivered in the third quarter and another 211K SF under construction. Tenants looking to grow are turning to suburban areas and converting vacant office and retail spaces that usually have cheaper rents and more parking than purpose-built medical office, industry executives said last week at Bisnow 's Boston Healthcare and Medical Campus Development event. Google Maps Beacon Capital Partners is converting 90K SF of office at 110 Worcester St. in Wellesley into clinical space. "The supply, especially in the infill of the Boston area, is so super tight," Colliers Executive Vice President Steve Woelfel said at the event, held at the Westin Boston Seaport District hotel. "What we continue to see is that growth of the suburbs." Many healthcare operators looking for space are working with tight budgets, making it difficult for new construction projects to pencil out. AEW Capital Management Vice President James Mayo-Smith said a lot of these tenants rely on private equity sponsors and institutional players to help make these build-outs possible. "The issue is the construction costs," Mayo-Smith said. "How do these healthcare organizations, if they're owning the real estate, afford to do it? And I think what we're starting to see is they'll partner with, whether it be private equity or other institutional landlords, to do the build-outs." Demand has never been stronger, especially as America's elderly population continues to grow and to require more care. Healthcare systems also understand that the need for suburban outposts is increasingly important to meet older patients closer to home. Bisnow/Taylor Driscoll Colliers' Steve Woelfel, AEW's James Mayo-Smith and Gamble Associates' David Gamble "There's inelastic demand, and we've got an aging population across the nation," Mayo-Smith said. Some medical office tenants are looking to other types of commercial real estate to expand their practices. Woelfel said conversions are happening in and around Boston as a way to address the lack of supply in the medical office market. Conversions are expected to account for a record 5.5% of all healthcare construction this year, according to CBRE . In the first half of the year, the firm found that 43% of medical office conversions were from retail properties, and another 42% were traditional office buildings. Greater Boston's traditional office market has far more empty space, with Avison Young reporting its availability rate last quarter at 21%. "The conversions are happening. The demand's there," Woelfel said. "I don't like to put medical office in the same sector as the office market, but the demand's always going to be there." "It's conversion of product, whether it be retail or office space," he added. "You're seeing more adaptive reuse of strip centers, cheap real estate." AEW has pursued a conversion project at its One Brigham Circle asset near Longwood Medical Center in Boston. The firm filed a proposed amendment to its master plan for the site to change uses for 67K SF in the property to allow clinic and accessory clinic uses. The Boston Planning Department approved the change in February. The Davis Cos . secured a 56K SF lease from Cambridge Health Alliance at One Cabot Road in Medford after the developer repositioned the building. The health system consolidated its services from its Assembly Square location into the new facility. Beacon Capital Partners shifted its proposed office-to-lab conversion at its Wellesley Gateway campus to include a 90K SF medical office project at 110 Worcester St. The project has already seen strong interest from tenants, Newmark Senior Managing Director Michael Greeley said. Bisnow/Taylor Driscoll Newmark's Michael Greeley, Limbach's Jerome Kapferer, HFA's Paul Sabal, Wise Construction's Chris Schena and Boston Medical Center's Nancy Hanright “There’s a kind of a gravity that starts to head towards new facilities, and they almost always get more popular," Greeley said. Woelfel said he worked with a fertility clinic to find space, signing a lease at an older office building. The tenant's landlord, an institutional owner, paid far more for the build-out than it probably anticipated but was willing to do so, Woelfel said. "They can do it, but not all landlords can," Woelfel said. "Not all landlords can do the build-out, and not all buildings work for it." Though there is a strong need for new space, healthcare systems are also grappling with limited capital and competing demands around their existing portfolio, technology investments, staffing and deferred maintenance. "The times are tough right now in healthcare in general, and that, capped with a year where politics are very volatile and cash is very low, we have a very strategic mindset in terms of capital investment and where and when we actually expand," Boston Medical Center Executive Director Nancy Hanright said at the event. items.title: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook
items.description: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook Written by Kenny Lee on November 18, 2026 What happened Housing starts jumped 9.9% from September to 1.309 million SAAR in October, up 2.8% from September last year. While starts in the West fell to the lowest in more than six years, the Midwest and South showed strength, rising 48.4% and 10.5%, respectively. However, sharp declines in new-construction permits indicate builders’ caution. Authorized units declined 7.4% to 1.295 million in October, with the single-family segment down sharply by 8.7%. All four Census regions saw declines in single-family construction permits. While notoriously volatile, multifamily housing starts nationwide jumped 25.5% to 433 thousand units in October. Although multifamily permits fell 5.2% from September to 475 thousand units in October, the latest pace is an improvement from this summer. Compared to last year, the three-month moving average of multifamily permits was up 3.5% from a year ago. Why it matters Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October , the largest year-over-year drop since 2023. Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes , the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane. The flipside of cooling buyer demand is skyrocketing renter demand. As elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead, renter demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Although the industry has been grappling with high new construction inventory over the past few years since the construction boom in 2022 and 2023, recent Zillow data shows market fundamentals started improving this year. The typical multifamily rent increased 2.5% year over year in October, compared to 1.3% growth one year ago, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Stronger rent growth reflects a resurgence of renter demand across the country. Recent gains in multifamily permits could be an early sign that the supply outlook is transitioning to growth. That said, it is worth noting that the Census Bureau's multifamily construction data relies on a survey with a small sample and is often subject to large revisions, and it will take additional data to see whether the recent gains indicate a new trend. Although developers still face challenging market conditions, such as high costs of construction financing, building materials, and skilled labor, a sustained improvement in multifamily supply will help alleviate the pressure on renters. items.description: Pending Home Sales Fall in October As Rates Hit 2026 Peak By Hannah Jones Nov 18, 2026 What did pending home sales look like in October? Pending home sales fell to another record-low, easing 4.7% in October, as mortgage rates hit a recent peak of 7.4%, and were down 16.7% from a year earlier. Rates have since eased back into the low 7% range, but October’s hot inflation data , released last week, is likely to push them higher again. Headline inflation rose 0.4% month over month, well above the 0.2% to 0.3% forecast, and core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. Markets now expect that a Fed rate hike is coming in December. Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued. What does this mean for buyers, sellers, and the housing market? All four regions saw declines both month over month and year over year, led by the West, where contract signings fell 6.9% for the month and 20.3% from a year earlier. The South followed with declines of 6.3% and 18.7%, then the Midwest with 2.7% and 14.0%. The Northeast had the smallest monthly drop, 0.8%, but was still down 11.1% from a year earlier. Even though all four regions saw dramatic cooling, the relative strength of the Midwest and Northeast are clear, due largely to still-scarce inventory conditions. Though all large metros saw pending home sales ease annually, the smallest drops were in Cincinnati (-4.7%), Austin (-9.7%) and Hartford, CT (-10.0%). Did the run-up to the November midterms keep buyers on the sidelines? Possibly. Some home shoppers may have held off to wait for the results, but rising rates are the more likely culprit . Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment. That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb. Affordability remains the limiting factor in today’s housing market. The typical mortgage-holder would see a $1,100 increase in their monthly payment if they bought a median-priced home today. Sellers have shown some flexibility, with lower asking prices and more price cuts , but buyers have not responded with much enthusiasm at these rates. Sellers are only willing to come down so far and buyers are only willing to stretch so far, and a gap still separates the two. As a result, transaction volume in October hit its lowest level in 16 years . There is an upside for buyers who can afford to act. With fewer shoppers in the market, they will face less competition for each listing, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more willing to negotiate on price, repairs, or closing costs.

items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 18, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share Month-Over-Month 4.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 16.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions WASHINGTON (November 18, 2026) – Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” October 2026 National Pending Home Sales 4.7% decrease month-over-month 16.7% decrease year-over-year October 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 0.8% decrease month-over-month 11.1% decrease year-over-year Midwest 2.7% decrease month-over-month 14.0% decrease year-over-year South 6.3% decrease month-over-month 18.7% decrease year-over-year West 6.9% decrease month-over-month 20.3% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Cincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, IN (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, IL-IN (-11.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-12.7%) Jacksonville, FL (-12.8%) Cleveland, OH (-12.8%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. items.title: New Construction Gives Mixed Signals in October
items.description: New Construction Gives Mixed Signals in October By Joel Berner Nov 18, 2026 October 2026 New Residential Construction What happened New residential construction sent some mixed signals in October and saw a recent trend of stronger permitting activity reverse itself. Permits fell 7.4% month over month and 8.7% year over year, while starts rose 9.9% from a weak September readout and 2.8% from their level last October. Completions themselves were mixed, rising 6.5% month over month but falling 10.4% year over year. The challenges facing builders have not subsided, and while there are some glimmers of hope in the housing starts figures, it must be noted that the current pace of single family home starts is still below last year’s actual total. This month’s data is an improvement, but from a very low baseline readout in both September and last October. Where it happened New housing units permitted for construction fell to their lowest level since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in May 2020. The pullback was most evident for single family homes, which fell 8.7% month over month and 12.9% year over year, while multifamily fell just 5.2% month over month and 0.4% year over year. Permitting was the lone bright spot in September’s new construction data release, but this month it comes as a disappointment. Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it’s rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand. This month’s data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on. Regionally, only the Midwest posted any kind of a gain in permitting, though that was concentrated in the multifamily space rather than single family. The other regions all saw a slowdown, most notably the West, which saw 20.0% fewer permits issued than it did this time last year. Housing starts had a better month in October following a very weak September. Gains in the Midwest (up 48.4% month over month and 17.2% year over year) and South (up 10.5% month over month and 12.2% year over year) offset losses in the Northeast (down 20.8% month over month and 34.5% year over year) and West (down 2.6% month over month and 11.6% year over year). Overall, multifamily projects pulled most of the weight for this improvement, rising 25.5% from September and 22.0% from last October while single family projects rose just 4.0% from September and fell 3.2% from last October. Nationwide asking rents finally broke their streak of falling for over 3 years while for-sale home listings have seen prices falling for all of 2026, so it makes sense for builders to be targeting large apartment building projects rather than single family homes. Completions improved month over month but remained below last year’s levels for both single family (up 6.3% month over month, down 10.7% year over year) and multifamily (up 9.0% month over month, down 9.0% year over year) projects. Again, it’s important to note that the current pace of completions (1,272,000 units) is still well below last year’s total (1,488,500 units), meaning that fewer new homes are coming onto the market. Regionally, the Midwest (+17.2%) and West (+3.7%) posted year-over-year gains while the Northeast (-34.5%) and South (-17.6%) saw significant pullback from last October. What does this mean for homebuyers, sellers, homeowners, and the housing market If you focus on home starts, this month’s new construction data is a welcome improvement from last month’s, but zooming out for more context shows a residential construction industry that is still struggling to find its footing. Builder confidence is at a 14-year low, and softening permits will put downward pressure on starts and completions in the months to come. In a country facing a supply gap of over four million homes, this represents a step in the wrong direction.

items.title: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER
items.description: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER Single-family leasing activity increased as rental prices edged higher HOUSTON -- (November 18, 2026) -- Houston-area renters kept the market moving in October, leasing more homes than a year ago even as rental prices edged higher. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Rental Market Update, 3,850 single-family homes were leased, a 3.5% increase from 3,720 in October 2025. A healthy supply of rental homes helped keep prices relatively stable. The average lease price for a single-family home rose just 1.2% to $2,293, compared to $2,266 in October 2025. "With affordability still top of mind, many people are taking a closer look at their housing options and what works best for their budgets," said HAR Chair-Elect Kat Robinson with SERHANT. "As we head toward the end of the year, that will continue to play a big role in whether people decide to rent or buy. For renters, it's encouraging to see that prices haven't changed much from last year." Townhomes and condominiums also saw an increase in leasing activity. A total of 638 properties were leased in October, up 9.1% from 585 a year earlier. The average lease price rose 4.0% to $1,943, while the median price increased 2.9% to $1,800. Rental inventory in this segment continued to expand. New listings increased 1.7% to 1,143 properties, while active listings rose 3.3% to 2,387. Townhomes and condominiums spent an average of 48 days on the market, one day longer than a year ago. items.description: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023 By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Nov 18, 2026 Highlights October 2026 marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023. The change was modest with the median asking rent rising by just $1 (+0.1%) from October 2025 to $1,692. Rents continue to split the difference between their recent highs and prepandemic level. They are down $82 (-4.6%) from summer 2022 peak, and up $221 (+15%) from pre-pandemic level. Rent rebounded in larger units, while studio rents continue to soften: Studio: $1,411, down $17 (-1.2%) YoY 1-bed: $1,566, up $1(+0.1%) YoY 2-bed: $1,889, up $5 (+0.3%) YoY In 2026Q3, multifamily deliveries have returned to pre-pandemic levels as the 2021–2022 boom cohorts clear. Looking ahead, a cooling in starts suggests that new rental supply is likely to stay modest in the near term. Completions: 330,000, down 26% YoY Under Construction: 674,000, down 2.7% YoY Starts: 403,000, down 9.2% YoY All U.S. regions share the national pattern of cooling completions but differ in what comes next based on starts and the under-construction pipeline: the Northeast is rebuilding, the Midwest and South are easing from elevated levels, and the West looks the most likely to tighten. In October 2026, the median asking rent rose 0.1% year over year, the first annual increase since June 2023. Median asking rent for 0–2 bedroom properties across the 50 largest metro areas was $1,692, about $221 (15%) above the pre-pandemic level but $82 (-4.6%) below the August 2022 peak. Median asking rents fell year over year for more than three years, and the 2021–2022 multifamily construction boom was the main driver of the decline. Projects started in those years were delivered in 2023–2025 and added supply that held rents down. According to the Housing Vacancy Survey, the rental vacancy rate reached 7.6% in 2026Q3, the highest level since early 2014. However, as construction activity unwinds, the downward pressure on rents from new supply has eased. At the same time, elevated borrowing costs may be supporting rental demand by keeping more households renting. The path ahead largely depends on whether new multifamily deliveries remain strong enough to outpace that demand. Larger units see rents increase In October 2026, the median asking rent for two-bedroom units rose 0.3% year over year, the first annual increase since May 2023. At $1,889, the national median for two-bedroom units is $82 (4.2%) below its July 2022 peak. Even after more than three years of softness, it remains $299 (18.8%) above its level seven years ago. The rent for one-bedroom units increased 0.1% in October 2026 on a year over year basis, and now stands at $1,566. This was the first month of annual rent growth since June 2023. Rent was $95 (-5.7%) lower than the peak observed during August 2022, but still $191 (13.9%) higher than in October 2019. In October 2026, the median asking rent for studios fell by 1.2%, marking the 39th consecutive month of annual declines. The median rent of studios was $1,411 in October, down by $73 (-4.9%) from its peak, seen in Fall 2022. Nevertheless, the median asking rent for studios was still $141 (11.1%) higher than seven years ago. items.description: New Home Lot Supply Index The New Home Lot Supply Index provides an unrivaled look into the lot markets across the country, offering a current quarter snapshot as well as insight into the directional trend. This report details data for the third quarter of 2026. November 18, 2026 – 4 min read Table of Content: Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index (LSI) for 3Q26, rose for the ninth consecutive quarter and showed lot supply loosened both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter across the United States. The index is a residential real estate indicator based on the number of single-family vacant developed lots (VDL) and the rate at which those lots are absorbed via housing starts. The New Home LSI came in at 88.5 for 3Q26, representing a 20.8% increase from 3Q25. This quarter, the market continued to be rated “appropriately supplied.” On a quarter-over-quarter basis, supply increased by 3.9% from 2Q26. The LSI counts the total vacant developed lot supply and adjusts it for overall starts activity. “The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” said Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market. Affordability pressures and widespread incentives underscore the challenges builders face in converting demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market means availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction; it does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost challenges have disappeared.” In 2Q26, the LSI sat right on the boundary between "slightly undersupplied" and "appropriately supplied." However, the upward movement in Q3 solidified the national rating as “appropriately supplied.” In 3Q26, lot supply loosened year-over-year across all major metropolitan areas Zonda tracks, except Boise. For markets that saw an increase in lot supply, the average year-over-year gain was significant at +32%. More markets trended up and were rated “appropriately supplied” or “oversupplied” in the third quarter, but 12 out of 30 were still categorized as “significantly undersupplied.” The markets where land supply loosened the most on a year-over-year basis were Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle. Boise was the only market where local lot supply tightened compared to 3Q25, falling from 65.7 to 51.9, joining one of 12 markets rated “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed ratings this quarter, as outlined in the chart below: Zonda also records future lots through the stages of development. The stages range from raw land through streets in, which is the last step before the lot becomes a vacant developed lot. Zonda groups the last few stages into a classification called total upcoming lots, which typically indicates delivery over the next 12-18 months. Total upcoming lots in 3Q26 increased 1.0% year-over-year and 1.6% quarter-over-quarter. These types of lots in the third quarter were down 12.2% from the 2022 peak but were up 23.4% compared to the same quarter in 2019. Among total upcoming lots, roadwork was down 15.3% year-over-year. Roadwork is comprised of the two smaller stages—streets paved and streets in—and represents the last step in lot development. Lots in the excavation stage were up 8.6% year-over-year, and those with equipment on site were up 5.7%. The largest share of total upcoming lots were in the excavation stage in 3Q26, totaling 416K. These lots have an expected delivery between 2Q27 and 3Q27 (the range represents different timeframes from local entitlement processes). Note, not all of the lots in excavation will match Zonda’s estimated timeline. “The development pipeline is edging higher, but the mix of activity matters,” Fergus said. “More lots are in excavation and equipment-on-site stages than a year ago, while fewer are in the final roadwork stages. That points to continued investment in future communities, but an uneven flow of near-term deliveries. Builders will need to weigh today’s softer demand environment against the time required to prepare lots for future construction.” Get a first look at Land AI Get a first look at Zonda Land AI on December 10th. items.title: Single-Family Starts Post Modest Monthly Rebound Amid Challenging Conditions
items.description: Single-Family Starts Post Modest Monthly Rebound Amid Challenging Conditions November 18, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Single-family housing starts edged up in October but still posted the year’s second-slowest pace, as builders face elevated financing and material costs, persistent labor shortages, and buyers holding back amid economic uncertainty. Single-family permits, the most important indicator in this report, declined to their lowest monthly pace since January 2023, reflecting continued weakness in single-family construction. Overall housing starts increased 9.9% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.31 million units, according to a report from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the U.S. Census Bureau. This pace reflects the number of housing units builders would begin over the next twelve months if October’s activity were sustained. Within the total, single-family starts increased 4.0% to an 864,000 seasonally adjusted annual rate. However, single-family starts were down 3.2% compared to October 2025. On a year-to-date basis, single-family starts were down 4.6%, reflecting continued challenges facing home builders . Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units. Multifamily starts, which include apartment buildings and condominiums, increased 23.6% from September to October to an annualized 445,000 pace. The three-month moving average for multifamily construction has trended lower to 401,000 units, but activity is 17.1% higher compared to year-earlier levels. Regionally, on a year-to-date basis, combined single-family and multifamily starts were 3.8% higher in the Northeast, 0.2% higher in the South, 0.7% lower in the Midwest, and 6.7% lower in the West. Single-family starts declined across all four regions, reflecting ongoing challenges amid elevated construction costs and persistent housing affordability pressures. The total number of housing units under construction stood at 1.27 million in October, down 3.0% from a year earlier. Single-family homes under construction stood at 581,000 units, a 2.5% year-over-year decline. Multifamily units under construction slowed to 691,000 units, down from peaks above 1 million units in December 2023 and 3.5% lower than a year ago. Single-family completions edged up to an annualized rate of about 900,000 units but came down 10.7% from a year earlier. Multifamily completions for buildings with five or more units declined 9.0% year-over-year to a 362,000-unit pace. However, compared to the previous month, completions were up 9.0%. On a year-to-date basis, total completions across both sectors were down 12.3%. Looking ahead, overall permits declined 7.4% in October to an annualized rate of 1.3 million units. Single-family permits declined 8.7% to a 772,000-unit rate, the lowest level since January 2023. Single-family permits were down 12.9% compared to October 2025 and are down 4.2% on a year-to-date basis. Multifamily permits declined 5.3% to an annualized 523,000 pace and are down 1.7% from a year earlier. Looking at regional permit data on a year-to-date basis, total permits were 8.7% higher in the Northeast, 2.0% higher in the Midwest, but 2.5% lower in the West and 4.4% lower in the South. items.title: Why 2027 may turn into a land negotiation year for homebuilders
items.description: In the early ’90s, I worked in Wells Fargo Bank ’s real estate workout group in Southern California. The aerospace collapse was crushing the local economy; Los Angeles County alone lost 400,000 jobs. Roughly 25% of WFB’s assets were in commercial real estate (including homebuilding), and another 25% in home mortgages, mostly in California. That was half the bank. Writing off loans and walking away to clean up the books wasn’t an option; we lacked the capital. So we fought for every penny. We asked for re-margins early on, short-term extensions and collected from borrowers before they ran out of money. We pursued personal guarantees and were willing to fight for them. I realize it is not what an audience of builders wants to hear, but everyone fights to survive. Bank of America was in a different position. It had less real estate concentration and wanted to expand by buying distressed banks, but it couldn’t until regulators were convinced it had moved past its own problems. So BofA cut deals or foreclosed, cleaning house. Its real estate recovery rate was far lower than ours. That doesn’t mean BofA was wrong. It simply had different incentives. Everyone knows Charlie Munger’s line, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.” We tend to apply it to individuals. But the coming year will be driven largely by company incentives. If you’re a builder, understanding the incentives of the companies across the table may be the most valuable market intelligence you can gather. Why the coming year? As I’ve said before, I’m not a big fan of short-term market projections. Over longer time spans, demographics , the fundamental balance of supply and demand, and affordability play out; they’re directionally predictable, if not precise. The short term has so many unforeseeable temporary factors that it can, paradoxically, be harder to call. Strategy is for the long term; in the short run, it’s mostly tactics, adapting to what’s in front of you. But caution about predicting short-term conditions is different from dismissing contingency planning. Housing market conditions have clearly deteriorated. Whatever the cause (war, politics, rising rates or all of the above), I suspect we never had the correction we should have after rates spiked in ’22. A frozen-in-place resale market and the effectiveness of rate buydowns made the following years difficult, but less so than many of us expected. One of the most intriguing aspects is that I can’t recall a more difficult period in homebuilding (to be clear, I’ve been through far worse, twice) that had so little impact on the land market. The reason was the belief that land was in such short supply that builders couldn’t afford to give up what they had and would need to buy more. Builders weren’t staying in current deals because they necessarily made sense, nor were they buying new ones because they liked the prices. The attitude was: what’s the alternative? That belief rested on two assumptions. First, that today’s weakness is a short-term problem: the rate shock would wear off, and buying would pick up. Second, that long-term fundamentals hadn’t changed, so demand would rebound and buoy prices. Either could prove true, but I’m skeptical. As I’ve written over the past year, future demand looks weak relative to the past, not a temporary dip but the start of a regime change. Once that becomes conventional wisdom, why would builders feel the need to control six to seven years of lots? Remember when three to four was considered plenty? Why won’t that be the case again? The land demand rotation I think 2027 is the year land prices will correct, not just terms but real prices. It’s current economics meeting a dawning recognition that the future will need fewer lots. Beyond a few year-end closings, not much will happen in the rest of 2026, and some will wait to see whether a magic spring rebound arrives. But over the last few months, we’ve seen a sharp downgrade in builder expectations for next year. Few expect things to improve soon. The public builders reinforce this. Many are eliminating forecasts or revising unit counts downward. Much like the difference between making a dollar and losing a dollar, which is much bigger than two dollars, once a builder admits it won’t be growing, it becomes much easier to walk from some positions. Once that threshold is crossed, Wall Street cares far less whether a builder shrinks 2% or 6%. Reasonable people can differ on this; there are multiple paths forward. But I think the odds are high enough to warrant contingency planning. If I’m right, what happens? To start, many land bankers (not the old vets, but the newcomers) will learn they weren’t offering a credit product. Like it or not, they’re in real estate and have taken real estate risk. Too many fundamentals in that business were stretched on the belief that big builders wouldn’t walk en masse . Expect meaningful re-trades, not just extensions. Meanwhile, land sellers will hear builders say they have options and don’t need to rush: “We’ll pay less and take them down on a rolling schedule with a 3% annual escalator. We can’t pay a land banker 10% to hold them; the margin’s too thin.” That’s where incentives come in. How each negotiation goes will depend heavily on the incentives of the companies involved, and each company has multiple layers. Using land bankers as an example, here are a few questions worth addressing. How are their asset management fees calculated and collected? As a percentage of revenue, assets (write-downs matter), or cost? Are they amortized over the deal’s life, or literally eat-what-you-kill, paid at closing? Last cycle, it wasn’t uncommon for equity funds to earn asset management fees based on revenue, with half taken up front and the rest amortized over the deal’s projected life. items.title: Nearly Nine in 10 Columbus-Area Residents Call Housing Affordability a Serious Problem, New Survey Finds
items.description:
Nearly Nine in 10 Columbus-Area Residents Call Housing
           Affordability a Serious Problem, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Columbus-area residents
COLUMBUS, Ohio – November 18, 2026 – Nearly nine in 10 Columbus-area residents say housing
affordability is a serious problem, and more than half have considered moving because of housing costs,
according to a new survey. Yet fewer than one in four are aware that Congress recently passed federal
legislation, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built
single-family rental homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: Nearly 90% of Columbus-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 55% have considered moving because of housing costs,
       including 30% who have considered leaving Ohio altogether.
   ●   Essential workers are feeling it: 63% say it is hard for teachers, nurses, police officers and
       firefighters to afford to live in the communities where they work.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 69% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   A majority of residents support new rental housing: 57% of Columbus-area residents support
       building more rental homes, 2-to-1 over those opposed.
   ●   Renters choose community over commute: By more than four to one, Columbus renters would
       rather rent a single-family home in the community they want than buy a larger home farther from
       work and family (46% to 10%). Two-thirds support building more single-family rentals to make
       that possible.

“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman, CEO
of the National Rental Home Council.

The findings come as Ohio policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following federal action
this past summer. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act authorized several new programs,
streamlined existing programs, like the HOME grant program, and placed limits on large institutional
investors from purchasing existing single-family homes.

“As state policymakers look ahead to 2027,” Todman said, “the opportunity is to help families find a home
that works for them, close to the jobs and communities they’ve built their lives around.”

About the survey

The survey of 600 Columbus-area residents was conducted via Pollfish in October 2026.

items.title: October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle
items.description: October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle by John Yellig November 18, 2026 October's pending home sales fell to what could be the nadir of this housing cycle — or it could represent just another step on the path of many would-be homeowners giving up altogether, the National Association of REALTORS® said. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” Pending sales fell 4.7% from September and 16.7% from October 2026 on a national basis. Regionally, contract signings were down across the board on monthly and yearly bases. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun said. Even the strongest markets in recent memory saw declines. These metros saw the smallest declines: Cincinnati, Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, Texas (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Connecticut (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, Indiana (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, Illinois-Indiana (-11.9%) Pittsburgh (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, Tennessee (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, New York (-12.7%) Jacksonville, Florida (-12.8%) Cleveland (-12.8%) “Buyers everywhere are running into the same affordability wall, with contract signings falling in every region," First American Financial Senior Economist Sam Williamson said. items.title: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid
items.description: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid The rule could displace tens of thousands of people, housing organizations say. A lawsuit claims the change is illegal and unconstitutional. Published Nov. 18, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google A U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule finalized Nov. 12, 2026, requires tenants receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 2 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development finalized a rule Nov. 12 requiring households receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. The rule, which goes into effect Dec. 14, effectively ends prorated federal housing assistance, which based the level of assistance on the number of eligible family members in the household. The new regulation could impact housing assistance for as many as 80,000 people, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A lawsuit challenging the rule’s legality was filed in the U.S. Central District of California Monday. Dive Insight: Nearly 9 million people participate in HUD housing assistance programs, which have long required immigration eligibility, according to NLIHC. HUD said the rule aims to bolster the agency’s “enforcement of the law” by requiring verification of immigration status for all household residents. It asserts that providing assistance to mixed-status households reduces the funds available to households that are fully eligible. “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said Nov. 10 in a press release. The agency said an audit of HUD-assisted households found around 200,000 tenants “ with incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.” David Dworkin, president and CEO of the National Housing Conference, called the regulation “a step backward.” “HUD’s concerns about immigration should be addressed through enforcement of existing laws, not by effectively evicting families who are here legally and creating expensive and burdensome processes for housing providers that are not capable of immigration enforcement,” Dworkin said in a statement. Of the approximately 80,000 individuals who could be displaced by the new requirements, nearly half are children, according to NLIHC. The lawsuit was filed by three unnamed plaintiffs residing in public housing or receiving housing assistance in Los Angeles County and two Los Angeles-area housing advocacy groups. It alleges the rule violates the Fair Housing Act, the Administrative Procedures Act and the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment guarantee of due process rights. items.title: Homeownership Remains a Key to Household Wealth
items.description: Homeownership Remains a Key to Household Wealth November 18, 2026 Jing Fu No Comments Homeownership continues to play an important role for household wealth accumulation in the United States. Beyond providing stability, owning a home allows households to build equity over time and accumulate a valuable financial asset. As highlighted in a previous blog post , the benefits of homeownership extend beyond wealth accumulation to include greater financial security, retirement stability, and broader household and community well-being. The latest Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances ( SCF ) 1 underscores the importance of housing in household finances. In 2025, primary residences accounted for more than one-quarter of total household assets, with an aggregate value of $47.2 trillion. The data also reveal a substantial wealth gap between homeowners and renters and show how important home equity varies across income and age groups. Primary Residences Remain an Important Household Asset Primary residences represent one of the largest components of U.S. household assets, exceeding several major financial and investment asset categories (Figure 1). In 2025, the aggregate value of primary residences reached $47.2 trillion, accounting for 26% of total household assets. This exceeded the value of other financial assets 2 (20%, or $36.3 trillion), retirement accounts (18%, or $33.4 trillion), and business interests (17%, or $31.5 trillion). Homeownership is also widely distributed among U.S. households. Nearly two-thirds (66%) owned their primary residence in 2025. By comparison, 55% of households held retirement accounts, while 20% owned stocks or bonds. Although other financial assets were held by 99% of households, this broad category includes checking accounts, money market accounts, and prepaid debit cards, which are often used primarily for everyday financial transactions rather than long-term wealth accumulation. The substantial share of household assets represented by primary residences highlights the importance of housing in the overall financial well-being of American households. Homeowners Continue to be Wealthier than Renters The importance of housing as a household asset is also reflected in the substantial wealth difference between homeowners and renters (Figure 2). In 2025, the median net worth of homeowner households was $458,900, compared with just $10,600 for renter households. This means that the median homeowner household had approximately 43 times the net worth of the median renter household. Between 2022 and 2025, median net worth among homeowners increased by 6%, while renters’ median net worth declined by 7%. The wealth gap extends beyond home equity. Homeowners also tend to hold greater amounts of financial assets, including retirement accounts, stocks, and other investments. In 2025, median financial assets among homeowners who held financial assets were $109,800, compared with $5,300 among renters who held financial assets. This difference suggests that the wealth advantage associated with homeownership is reflected in broader household balance sheets, not just housing wealth. It is worth noting that income, age, education, and other household characteristics also contribute to the observed wealth gap. These findings therefore illustrate the strong association between homeownership and greater household wealth rather than establishing homeownership as the sole cause of the difference. Home Equity Plays an Important Role for Lower-income and Older Households While homeowners generally have greater wealth than renters, the contribution of home equity to household wealth varies considerably across income and age groups (Figure 3). For many households, particularly those approaching or in retirement, accumulated home equity represents a substantial share of their overall wealth. The median share of wealth held in home equity generally increases with age and decreases with income. Among households age 75 and older, home equity accounts for 62% of wealth in the lowest-income group, compared with just 16% among those in the highest-income group. A similar pattern appears among households age 65–74, where the median home equity share ranges from 40% for the lowest-income group to 15% for the highest-income group. These findings highlight the importance of housing equity as a source of financial security later in life. For lower-income older households, accumulated home equity can represent a particularly important store of wealth and a potential source of financial flexibility during retirement. However, this pattern is not universal across all age and income groups. Several younger, lower-income groups have a median home equity share of zero, reflecting the fact that many households in these groups do not own a home. This variation illustrates how differences in access to homeownership, as well as the ability to accumulate housing equity, shape the composition of household wealth. Mortgage-free Homeowners have Accumulated More Housing Equity and Wealth The extent of housing wealth also depends on where households are in the mortgage repayment process. Comparing homeowners with and without outstanding mortgage debt provides another perspective on how home equity relates to overall household wealth (Figure 4). In 2025, almost two-thirds of homeowners had outstanding home-secured debt, while just over one-third owned their homes free of mortgage debt. As expected, homeowners who had paid off their mortgages held greater housing equity and higher overall net worth than those still carrying a mortgage. The median primary residence equity among mortgage-free homeowners was $300,000, compared with $205,000 among homeowners with outstanding mortgages. The difference was also evident in overall household wealth: mortgage-free homeowners had a median net worth of $605,700, compared with $417,730 for homeowners who still carried mortgage debt. items.title: Guild's Nora Guerra on helping baby boomers buy and rehab homes with reverse mortgages
items.description: Baby boomers represent 42% of homebuyers and 55% of sellers, according to the most recent data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), yet the mortgage industry has yet to fully account for their presence. That was the message shared last week by Nora Guerra, senior vice president of community lending solutions at Guild Mortgage , during the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)'s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio. Guerra — who previously worked at Freddie Mac , where she studied how homebuyers change by age group — told the audience that lenders have spent years chasing younger consumers while overlooking older, equity-rich groups who are moving frequently and are in need of help. "This 55-plus buyer, it's a main demographic buyer. Everybody has been so focused on the millennial — the older millennial, the younger millennial — and now the Gen Zer ," she said. Jolted by the pandemic Before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, boomers were largely staying put and had few incentives to move, Guerra said. But that changed quickly as single-family home price appreciation skyrocketed from 3.2% in 2019 to 11.3% in 2021 and 11.9% in 2022, according to HousingWire Data . That contributed heavily to home equity accumulation, with homeowners 62 and older now holding $15.34 trillion in housing wealth, according to NRMLA and RiskSpan . Additionally, the pandemic caused a rupture in many families' living situations. "They were sheltered in place. They couldn't see their loved ones, their grandchildren and their children, and it shook them very hard," Guerra said. Across years of research, Guerra has uncovered four distinct groups of older homebuyers: Family-focused movers who want to be closer to children, grandchildren and other family members Lifestyle-focused retirees, who seek to fulfill daily routines and may be strong candidates for renovation loans Financial-focused planners, who want their housing decisions to align with long-term plans like retirement Stay-put homeowners, who want to age in place in a familiar community but have hurdles to doing so Each of these groups are likely to need financing to accomplish their goals, she said. Reverse mortgages may offer a more cost-effective solution since they don't require a monthly payment, and they're often a fit for applicants who've been turned down for other types of mortgage credit. Reverse mortgage for purchase programs , in particular, can fulfill their needs. These products allow seniors to sell their current home and use the equity to buy a similar or more expensive property without monthly payments or the need to pay in cash. "They really don't know what options are out there, so they feel no one wants to finance me," Guerra remarked. According to NAR research cited by Guerra, senior homebuyers frequently utilize mortgages, but the trend wanes as the buyer grows older. The data shows that among 61- to 70-year-olds, 61% financed their purchase during the year ending in June 2025. The percentage dropped to 54% among 71- to 79-year-olds, and to 48% among those 80 and older. Focus on solutions, not challenges Guerra said mortgage professionals spend too much time discussing problems and not enough time on finding or developing solutions. This can be particularly unhelpful when working with house-rich, cash-poor clients who have significant equity but little in the way of savings or retirement funds. With these types of needs-based borrowers, reverse mortgage professionals should be asking about the cash they're looking to access for both everyday living expenses and unexpected expenses . Develop a cash-flow plan based on what they have in their retirement accounts and other investments. Whether a client is considering a federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage or a proprietary reverse mortgage, counselors certified by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are a key resource to tap into. Guerra said she works with more than 200 counselors nationwide who "help educate and hold the hand of your parent, and tell them all about this program and how it works." Originators should ask direct questions about the client's preferences to pay for their next home, identify any assets they don't want to touch for that purpose, and offer comparisons of what the financial results will look like with a reverse mortgage versus a cash deal. Family members often fear there will be nothing left for them when their parent or grandparent dies. But planning ahead of time can help heirs to sell the home and keep any proceeds, or to repay the reverse mortgage and continue living there. Some lenders offer private-label solutions for these exact situations . Guerra also pointed to NAR data showing that 14% of recent home purchases were tied to multigenerational living situations. These clients often need their family involved when making decisions about reverse mortgages. Adult children want to protect their parents' assets, so originators should include relatives early in the process. "Mom and dad haven't bought a home in the last 10 or 15 years due to lack of inventory. Grandma and grandpa haven't bought a home in the last 15 to 20 years due to the same reason," Guerra told the audience. "Multigenerational living is what we're seeing on these 1003 (loan applications) — lots of grandparents cosigning for their millennial and Gen Z grandchildren if they can afford it, but also lots of gift letters." items.title: Another record low for pending home sales, NAR index drops to 63
items.description: Pending home sales fell to yet another record low in October, according to data published by the National Association of Realtors (NAR) on Wednesday. According to the report, NAR’s Pending Home Sales Index fell to a reading of 63 in October, down 4.7% from a month ago and 16.7% a year ago. An index value of 100 is equivalent to the level of contract signings in 2001. Despite the new record low, NAR’s chief economist is optimistic that things may turn around in November. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, a s mortgage rates appear to have topped out ,” Yun said in a statement. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s. It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” HousingWire Data , which is more up to date, shows that for the week ending Nov. 13, 2026, 295,621 single family homes were pending in the U.S., down 14.1% from a year ago. Pending home sales declined in all four major regions on both a year-over-year and month-over-month basis in October, according to NAR data. The West posted both the largest annual and monthly declines, dropping 20.3% from a year ago and 6.9% a month ago to an index value of 45.8. The Northeast (58.5) posted the smallest monthly and annual declines at 0.8% and 11.1%, respectively. Despite falling 18.7% annually and 6.3% from a month ago, pending home sales in the South remained the closest to 2001 levels, with an index reading of 74.5. Meanwhile, pending sales in the Midwest (65.5) fell 2.7% month-over-month and 14.0% from a year ago. Locally, pending home sells fell annually in all 50 of the largest metro areas analyzed, with the smallest declines occurring inCincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%), Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) and Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) according to data from Realtor.com Economics . Looking ahead, with the Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates at their meeting in December, economists believe a near-term rebound in contract signings is unlikely. “A meaningful rebound looks unlikely any time soon, with further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve likely to keep a floor under rates as it keeps up its fight against inflation,” Sam Williamson, First American ’s senior economist, said in a statement. “While those hikes could eventually open the door to lower rates, but it will take convincing evidence that inflation is retreating toward the Fed's target. In the meantime, life events will keep some households moving, even as high rates discourage move-up and other discretionary moves and give some first-time buyers a little more reason to wait. Higher incomes and slower price growth may restore some buying power, but rates will limit how much of it turns into sales.” Related More: National Association of Realtors Pending Home Sales
